canonical_statement: This was a single-center retrospective observational cohort study at a large tertiary-care academic medical center with institutional review board approval.
The ABW dosing cohort used adjusted body weight as the initial heparin dosing weight, calculated as IBW + 0.4 × (TBW − IBW).

concept.text: IV unfractionated heparin dosed using adjusted body weight (ABW)

exposures.details: Initial dosing weight selected as adjusted body weight; ABW = IBW + 0.4 × (TBW − IBW).

canonical_statement: The TBW dosing cohort used total body weight as the initial heparin dosing weight.

concept.text: IV unfractionated heparin dosed using total body weight (TBW)

exposures.details: Initial dosing weight selected as total body weight.

canonical_statement: The institutional thrombosis nomogram used an initial heparin infusion of 18 units/kg/hour with or without an 80 units/kg loading dose, with neither the initial bolus nor the initial rate capped.
The heparin order defaulted to recorded TBW for dose determination, but providers could change the dosing weight during order entry based on clinical expertise.
Heparin was monitored using HCV, with a therapeutic target of 0.3 to 0.7; the initial HCV was checked 6 hours after infusion initiation and subsequent timing followed the nomogram.
For HCV <0.2 or 0.2, the thrombosis nomogram specified a 5000-unit bolus and an infusion increase of 2 or 1 units/kg/hour, respectively, with repeat testing at least 6 hours after the new rate.
For therapeutic HCV 0.3-0.7, the nomogram specified no bolus, hold, or rate change and the next HCV the following morning.

For HCV above target, the nomogram used stepwise rate reductions and holds: 0.8-1.1 decrease 1 unit/kg/hour; 1.2-1.5 hold 60 minutes and decrease 2; 1.6-1.8 hold 60 minutes and decrease 3; >1.8 hold 90 minutes and decrease 4; two consecutive HCV values >1.8 prompted stopping the infusion and contacting the prescriber.

Patients were identified through the Carolina Data Warehouse for Health and study data were collected from the electronic medical record, including demographics, heparin orders/administration, laboratory values, and bleeding signs.
The primary outcome was therapeutic HCV at the first laboratory check after heparin initiation.

concept.text: Initial therapeutic HCV

outcome.definition: HCV within the therapeutic range at the first laboratory check after heparin initiation.

canonical_statement: Secondary outcomes included therapeutic HCV at any time, time to first therapeutic HCV, infusion rate required for therapeutic HCV, HCV category at 24 hours, dose adjustments in the first 24 hours, and any supratherapeutic HCV during therapy.
Major bleeding was defined using ISTH criteria: fatal bleeding, symptomatic bleeding in a critical area or organ, hemoglobin decrease ≥2 g/dL, or transfusion of ≥2 units of whole blood or red cells.

concept.text: Major bleeding

outcome.definition: ISTH major bleeding definition used by the study.

canonical_statement: Efficacy endpoints for new, residual, or recurrent thrombosis were not evaluated because follow-up imaging was not routinely performed.

canonical_statement: Obesity was stratified as Class 1 BMI 30-<35 kg/m², Class 2 BMI 35-<40 kg/m², and Class 3 BMI ≥40 kg/m².

Categorical data were analyzed with chi-square testing, continuous data with unpaired t-test or Mann-Whitney U testing, and statistical significance was set at P<.05; no power calculation was performed because dosing-weight use was imbalanced.
Of 688 patients screened, 477 were included in the primary analysis: 453 (94.9%) in the TBW cohort and 24 (5.1%) in the ABW cohort; Figure 1 reports 211 exclusions.

canonical_statement: ABW versus TBW dosing did not produce a statistically significant difference in initial therapeutic HCV attainment, although the authors noted that the limited sample size could not exclude a meaningful difference.
The authors interpreted the higher frequency of supratherapeutic HCV with TBW dosing as a reason to consider empiric heparin dose adjustment in obese patients.
For Class 3 obesity, the authors stated that the 72.5% versus 38.5% supratherapeutic-HCV rates with TBW versus ABW dosing argue for considering empiric dose adjustment at heparin initiation.

Because the ABW cohort required a lower therapeutic infusion rate when normalized to TBW, the authors inferred that TBW-normalized dose requirements decrease as weight and BMI increase and that dosing-weight adjustment may be a more consistent empiric strategy.
The authors recommended prospective studies comparing dosing-weight selection, initial bolus or infusion-rate modifications, and dose capping in obese patients.

The small and markedly imbalanced cohorts limited statistical power to detect clinically meaningful differences and limited evaluation of relevant subgroups and patient-centered outcomes such as major bleeding.
ABW dosing was selected by provider preference, creating potential treatment-selection confounding and baseline between-group differences.
The study design could not exclude a provider effect in which some clinicians preferentially used ABW and others preferentially used TBW.
The retrospective design and missing data prevented evaluation of additional clinical efficacy outcomes and all potential risk factors for bleeding, VTE development, or altered HCV values.
The single-center setting and use of a specific heparin order set and nomogram may limit generalizability.
In the study conclusion, ABW compared with TBW did not increase attainment of therapeutic anticoagulation at the first monitoring timepoint.
Increased supratherapeutic anticoagulation with TBW dosing was stated to warrant consideration of empiric dose adjustment in obese patients.
